A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same attribution method and CLIP study. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and matchable, including Appendices A–D in v1 and A–F in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original grounding evaluations, fine-tuning comparisons, class-wise analyses and hard-negative caption experiments in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds attribution-method comparisons, perturbation experiments and a systematic failure analysis.

M1.justification: The integrated-Jacobian construction, reference inputs, attribution product and slicing procedure remain the same in Equations 1–11. Renaming feature-pair attributions as second-order attributions and adding implementation explanations do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: COCO, Flickr30k and HNC coverage is retained. v2 adds distinct perturbed-input scenarios involving image-patch and caption-token insertion or deletion, while introducing no new source dataset or application domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct evaluations against Interaction-CAM, InteractionLIME, ITSMout and ITSMhidden in Tables 1, 2a and 5, plus Random in perturbation tests. Figure 1 also introduces qualitative first-order comparisons. These empirical attribution-method comparisons were absent from v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces conditional insertion/deletion procedures for both modalities and evaluates their AUCs. Although PGE and PGA correspond to the earlier gamma and rho metrics, v2 replaces the reported gamma>0.5 summary with a claimed median PGE while retaining its numerical entries. This is an unexplained reported metric change, not evidence of rerunning experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained fine-tuning, class-wise and hard-negative analyses, v2 adds perturbation-based attribution tests. It also replaces illustrative failure discussion with categorization of approximately 200 low-PGE examples per model for Laion, OpenAI and DFN, reporting category frequencies and extensive examples in Figures 7 and 12.

E5.justification: Class-wise standard deviations and the stochastic-dominance testing framework are retained. New perturbation curves in Figures 3, 16 and 17 contain shaded bands, but v2 never defines their meaning or computation. It is therefore unclear whether these introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice or reuse existing variability reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds perturbation AUCs, baseline grounding scores, hard-negative similarity-score changes and failure-category frequencies. For example, Table 1 reports Laion CID AUCs of 65.94 for the proposed method and 91.39 for Interaction-CAM. Original grounding numbers largely persist, but some v2 results conflict: Laion/Flickr30k PGA is 61.8 in Table 2a and 63.6 in Table 5, without an explained setting difference.

T1.justification: The central derivation and the one-step GradCAM-style simplification already appear in v1. New Appendix E adds a formal specification of InteractionLIME's bilinear surrogate, weighted optimization objective and similarity weighting in Equations 17–19; it does not introduce a new proof for the proposed method.

C1.justification: v2 adds systematic failure categories to the principal contributions stated in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. The central claims about general dual-encoder attribution, fine-grained grounding, negative mismatch contributions and improvement through in-domain tuning remain substantively intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of comparator weaknesses, including InteractionLIME's text/image imbalance and optimization sensitivity, and acknowledges distribution-shift problems in perturbation tests. It interprets the categorized failures as evidence of difficulty separating correlated objects and drops v1's specific conjecture about OpenAI pretraining containing COCO/Flickr30k. The original approximation and contextualization limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies attribution to second-last hidden representations with 50 integration steps. Appendices E and F document baseline sampling and optimization settings, latent perturbations, PyTorch hooks and batched Jacobian computation. These substantially improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments. Code release is promised, not demonstrated.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial CLIP-explainability discussion and positions the method against InteractionLIME, Interaction-CAM, ITSM and numerous other approaches. It explicitly acknowledges prior caption-image interaction explanations and develops distinctions involving surrogate optimization and gradient simplification, extending v1's positioning around Siamese-encoder attribution.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change, and the introduction and discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Experiments are reorganized into attribution evaluation and model analysis, formerly separate analyses become paragraphs within that structure, and the appendices expand to include baseline and implementation explanations.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a slicing schematic and comparison panels, merges the original intra-modal figures, combines plots with examples, and moves original main-text material into the appendices. New baseline tables, perturbation plots and failure-example grids substantially change the presentation. Typography, table organization and page layout are also redesigned.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's lack of direct attribution-method comparisons and adds useful perturbation evidence and implementation details, improving validation and reproducibility. However, it reuses gamma>0.5 values as purported medians, reports inconsistent corresponding Laion results, and relabels the original DFN class-wise plot as Laion. These reporting problems weaken the grounding evidence. The additional perturbation tests and implementation guidance support a limited net improvement, but the quantitative inconsistencies prevent a stronger assessment.
